thread:
maria: Hey team — Escalation from AcmeHealth. Their nightly ETL has been intermittently failing since last night with 403s when the CI job tries to pull secrets (KMS) using our CI service account token. PR builds succeed, only scheduled runs fail. Can someone help triage? :raising_hand:

alex: Thanks for the ping. Do we have an example log from the failing run? Is it always 403 or does it sometimes vary?

maria: Always 403 in the logs. Here's the failure snippet the customer pasted:

```
Error: GET https://kms.redwood.example.com/v1/projects/... 403
{"error":"access_denied","error_description":"token audience mismatch: expected \"https://kms.redwood.example.com/\" got \"https://github.com/orgs/AcmeHealth/actions\""}
```

ramesh: Interesting — that looks like an `aud` mismatch on the OIDC token. PR builds use `pull_request` workflows (repo-level OIDC) which set audience to our minting service, but scheduled workflows apparently have a different audience string. GitHub Actions scheduled runs set audience differently unless `id-token: audiences` is specified in the workflow.

joel: Can we reproduce locally? Maria, can you share the failing workflow run URL and a redacted job log? If we can exchange the OIDC token via our token-exchange endpoint we can inspect the `aud` claim.

maria: Pasted run: https://github.com/AcmeHealth/etl/actions/runs/987654321 (customer masked org, they allowed support to view). Redacted relevant bits above. They also said they didn't set `id-token: audiences:` in their scheduled job.

alex: Quick repro steps for us to confirm: 1) Trigger a scheduled workflow in an internal repo without `id-token: audiences`; 2) Use `actions/github-script` to `id-token` and print it; 3) Decode `aud` with `jq`/`jwt` or jwt.io. Example extraction command we use: 

```
# in a runner
curl -s --request POST \ 
  --url "https://token-exchange.redwood.internal/oidc" \ 
  --data '{"raw_id_token":"'$GITHUB_ID_TOKEN'"}' | jq -r .aud
```

(we redact exact internal endpoints in public threads)

ramesh: Confirmed behavior: scheduled runs default the `aud` to `https://github.com/orgs/<org>/actions` which does not match the audience our token-minting policy expects. The minting service rejects tokens whose `aud` doesn't match `allowed_audiences`. That's why PRs (aud matches) work and scheduled jobs fail.

maria: OK that explains it. What's the fix we should suggest to the customer? They want minimal change.

alex: Short-term workaround: add `id-token: write` + explicit audiences to the scheduled workflow so GitHub will mint an id_token with our expected audience. Example snippet for their workflow YAML:

```
permissions:
  id-token: write
jobs:
  nightly:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Request id token
        uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Exchange token
        run: |
          echo "Requesting id token"
          export TOKEN=$(curl -s -H "Accept: application/vnd.github+json" \
            -X POST https://gh.api/actions/requests/... )
```

(we redact exact internal endpoints in public threads)

ramesh: We should avoid leaking GH syntax mistakes. I'll paste the recommended YAML to give to customers in support docs. For now, tell them to add: 

```
permissions:
  id-token: write
jobs:
  cron:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/github-script@v6
        with:
          script: |
            const token = await core.getIDToken({audience: 'https://kms.redwood.example.com/'});
            console.log(token);
```

This ensures `aud` matches our allowed audience.

joel: Long-term, we should consider making our minting service accept both the canonical audience and the org-specific GH audience, but that could be a security regression. Better is to document the `aud` requirement and add a helpful error message pointing to the exact workflow snippet.

maria: AcmeHealth is asking if we can temporarily relax `allowed_audiences` for their account so they don't have to change tens of repos. What's the risk?

alex: Relaxing the audience check is risky — it widens which tokens can mint credentials. If we must support it, do it as a scoped exception tied to the customer's org and time-box it with an audit trail. Also require a short TTL on minted tokens.

ramesh: Alternative: we can provide a small Terraform module / GH workflow template they can drop into repos to fix all scheduled jobs quickly. That's low-risk and preferred. I'm happy to own a one-click script that patches their repos if they give org-level permissions.

maria: Customer asked about token TTLs — they saw some jobs succeed, then fail ~12h later. Could token caching be involved?

alex: Yes — if the runner or our caching layer stores credentials beyond the token expiry or uses a token minted with an audience that gets rotated out from our allowed list, you can get intermittent passes. Recommend: 1) ensure workflows request fresh id_tokens at job runtime; 2) don't cache long-lived derived credentials; 3) use short TTLs (e.g., <= 1h) for minted service-account tokens.

joel: Action items:
- ramesh: create a GH workflow template + docs with explicit `id-token` audience example and TTL guidance. (ETA: today EOD)
- alex: add a new support note to the KB with the exact error string matching `token audience mismatch` and the minimal YAML snippet. (ETA: tomorrow)
- maria: share the customer contact and confirm whether they want a scoped temporary exception.

ramesh: I'll also add an internal alert in the token-minting service to surface ambiguous `aud` values with a link to KB. That will reduce future escalations.

maria: Thanks all. I'll message AcmeHealth with the workaround snippet and ask if they'd like us to push a repo template. :pray:

ci-bot: Deployment probe: updated support KB entry draft pushed to `docs/support/oidc-audience.md` (internal).
